candidates.attacker_control: A malicious ZIP archive controls every `ZipEntry.getName()` (e.g. `../../../../home/user/.ssh/authorized_keys`, `../../etc/cron.d/x`, or backslash variants on Windows) and the entry payload bytes. Applications that extract untrusted uploads/archives with `ZipUtil.unpack(...)` or `Zips...unpack()` process these names verbatim; the default `IdentityNameMapper` returns the name unchanged and a custom NameMapper can also be a pass-through.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Searched the whole snapshot for containment/sanitization logic: no `normalize`, `getCanonicalPath`, `isValid`, `ZipEntryValidator`, or 'Slip' checks exist in any extraction path (canonical-path comparisons exist only in embedded commons-io copy/move helpers in FileUtilsV2_2.java). The default IdentityNameMapper is a pass-through and mapper output is also used unsanitized. `new File(parent, child)` does not let a Unix-style absolute child escape parent, so the practical vector is `..` segments (plus backslash separators on Windows), not leading '/'; `Zips.addFile` only strips a leading '/' when creating archives, which does not protect extraction. Java's `java.util.zip.ZipFile`/`ZipInputStream` do not filter traversal names. No tests are present in the snapshot to contradict this.
candidates.impact: Arbitrary creation/overwrite of files writable by the extracting process outside the intended extraction directory (config files, shell profiles, cron/systemd/startup scripts, other users' home directories). Depending on how the extracted content is subsequently used or executed, this can escalate to code execution or privilege escalation; at minimum it is a high-integrity compromise. Parent directories are also created (`forceMkdir`), so the attacker can create directory structures outside the target as well. Extracted ASi extra-field permissions (ZipUtil.java:1166-1168) can additionally mark attacker-written files executable.
candidates.prerequisites: The application calls a public extraction API (e.g. `ZipUtil.unpack(File, File)` at ZipUtil.java:938/957/975 or `unpack(InputStream, ...)` at 1044/1060/1076/1094, or the `Zips` fluent `unpack()` API which routes to `UnpackingCallback`) on an archive whose entry names/payloads are attacker-influenced, and the JVM process has write permission to the paths the traversal targets. A pre-validating caller-provided NameMapper would avoid it, but this is not enforced or documented as required.
candidates.root_cause: Extraction callbacks build destination paths as `new File(outputDir, zipEntry.getName())` (or the mapper output / unrooted name) and write entry contents there without verifying that the resolved path stays inside outputDir. Entry names containing `..` path segments (and, on Windows, backslash separators) escape the intended directory. No canonicalization/containment check or `..` rejection exists in the repository.
candidates.title: Zip Slip: unvalidated ZIP entry names allow arbitrary file write outside the extraction directory
candidates.trace: ZipUtil.unpack(File zip, File outputDir) -> unpack(...) -> iterate(zip, new Unpacker(outputDir, mapper), charset) (ZipUtil.java:977) -> iterate() enumerates `ZipFile.entries()` and calls action.process(is, e) (ZipUtil.java:502-508) -> Unpacker.process reads `zipEntry.getName()`, passes it through the mapper unchanged (IdentityNameMapper.java:31-33), builds `File file = new File(outputDir, name)` (ZipUtil.java:1152), creates parent directories (`FileUtils.forceMkdir(file.getParentFile())`, line 1157) and writes the entry via `FileUtils.copy(in, file)` (line 1163) -> commons/FileUtils.copy opens `new FileOutputStream(file)` (FileUtils.java:54). Because `../` segments are not removed and the result is never compared against the canonical outputDir, the write lands outside outputDir. The same sink pattern exists in BackslashUnpacker (lines 1210-1226), Unwraper (1260/1271) and Zips.UnpackingCallback (Zips.java:683/689/695).
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed: no archive was executed and no filesystem writes were performed. Exact exploitability depends on the calling application, the charset/mapper used, OS path semantics, and the extracting process's permissions; OS-specific behaviors (Windows drive/UNC names, symlink targets that may already exist under outputDir) were reasoned about from source but not tested. The repository contains only main sources (no test suite) in this snapshot.
candidates.weakness_type: Path traversal / Zip Slip (CWE-22) leading to arbitrary file overwrite

coverage_summary: All 54 files in the assigned snapshot were listed; the extraction and file-writing paths were read in depth (ZipUtil unpack/iterate/unpackEntry callbacks, Zips.UnpackingCallback/process, commons/FileUtils.copy, FileUtilsV2_2 forceMkdir/copy helpers, ZipEntryUtil permissions handling, ExtraFieldUtils/AsiExtraField parsing, IdentityNameMapper, pom.xml/Changelog version confirmation, README usage examples). Text searches covered sanitization (`normalize`, `getCanonicalPath`, `isValid`, 'Slip'), command execution, deserialization, and symlink creation; none exist in the runtime library. Large utility files (ZipUtil.java ~3300 lines, FileUtilsV2_2.java ~1200 lines) were sampled rather than read line-by-line outside the extraction-relevant regions.
limitations: No code was executed and no tests are included in the snapshot; findings are source-evidence based, not runtime-confirmed.
ZipUtil.java (100 KB) and FileUtilsV2_2.java (41 KB) were not read exhaustively; unread regions could contain additional issues, but the extraction path relevant to the candidate was fully traced.
Exploitability depends on caller behavior (whether untrusted archives are extracted and with what process privileges) and OS path semantics, which are outside this snapshot.

The candidate consolidates one root cause (unvalidated entry-name-to-path resolution). The BackslashUnpacker and Unwraper variants are treated as the same root cause rather than separate candidates per the one-candidate limit.

rejected_leads.lead: Attacker-controlled 'ASi Unix' (0x756e) extra field causes runtime exceptions during unpack: ExtraFieldUtils.parse accepts field lengths < 4 (ExtraFieldUtils.java:120-143), then AsiExtraField.parseFromLocalFileData does `new byte[length - WORD]` (AsiExtraField.java:373) and multiple fixed-offset reads (ZipLong/ZipShort), so malformed extra data can throw NegativeArraySizeException/ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; ZipEntryUtil.getZTFilePermissions only catches java.util.zip.ZipException (ZipEntryUtil.java:190-203).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible malformed-input DoS/uncaught-exception path, but impact is limited to aborting extraction (caught or propagated runtime exception) and it is a separate root cause from the path traversal; it was not selected as the single candidate. Not confirmed at runtime.

rejected_leads.lead: Attacker-controlled permissions: unpacking applies POSIX mode bits taken from the ASi extra field to the written file (ZipUtil.java:196-197, 1166-1168), which can set executable/world-writable bits.
rejected_leads.reason: It amplifies the impact of the zip-slip/arbitrary-write candidate but is a weaker standalone finding (bounded to 0777 bits, no setuid/setgid handling visible) and shares the same attacker-controlled archive entry surface; left out of the one-candidate limit.

rejected_leads.lead: Release shell scripts (get_release_commands.sh, oss-release.sh) and .travis.yml contain build/release command sequences.
rejected_leads.reason: Maintainer-side tooling, not reachable from library runtime and not exposed to attacker-controlled input; no evidence of an exploitable trust boundary.

summary: The snapshot is the pre-1.13 zt-zip library (pom.xml version 1.12). Every archive-extraction path resolves attacker-controlled ZIP entry names directly against the caller-supplied output directory with no `..`/containment validation, producing a classic Zip Slip arbitrary-file-write issue (CWE-22). The strongest candidate is this single root cause, present in ZipUtil.Unpacker, ZipUtil.BackslashUnpacker, ZipUtil.Unwraper, and Zips.UnpackingCallback, all reachable from public `unpack(...)` APIs documented in README. No sanitization, canonical-path check, or name validation exists anywhere in the extraction code.
